newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan shuts hog markets during mass slaughter.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan shuts hog markets during mass slaughter.

text.p: Taiwan on Monday ordered hog trading halted for three days at 19 of the island's 22 major hog wholesale centres as troops began slaughtering all pigs at farms infected by highly contagious foot and mouth disease.
"We are conducting a massive slaughter in 19 counties and trading must be halted to stop movements of pigs," an official of the cabinet's Council of Agriculture said.
Trading would be suspended on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday at wholesale centres in the 19 counties to ensure that meat from infected animals do not reach the market, the official said.
Officials hoped that the temporary trading suspension would ease public fears about contamination and thereby stabilise prices when trading resumes on Thursday.
The Taiwan Meats Trade Association has imposed a voluntary market recess until March 30 in an additional safety measure.
Local pork prices have plunged as much as 60 percent since the crisis erupted on March 20 and officials said it could shave half a percentage point off Taiwan's gross domestic product.

Farm experts backed by soldiers wearing protective clothing late on Friday began the process of slaughtering an estimated 100,000 or more hogs at farms stricken with the fatal disease, which is highly contagious and can spread through the air.
"The council has ordered the slaughter of all pigs at all infected farms," the official said. "Even if there is only one confirmed infection, we will have to eliminate all the pigs."
Humans cannot contract the disease but officials were concerned about a possible spread to other livestock, particularly Taiwan's large herd of dairy cows.

Taiwan television showed graphic footage of masked soldiers in white plastic suits wielding electric prods to stun pigs, then using bulldozers and back-hoes to dump the animals, many still alive, into giant pits.
The council banned pork exports on March 20 after confirming the outbreak in the island's large hog population, dealing a stunning blow to one of Taiwan's major export industries.
Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong told a parliamentary committee on Monday the crisis could reduce the island's 1997 GDP by 0.5 percentage points from the forecast 6.28 percent.

"The impact from the foot and mouth disease outbreak could mean that the island's gross domestic product could lose a half a percentage point in 1997," Sheu said. The council estimated six million of the 14 million hogs raised each year in Taiwan were exported.
Japan, Taiwan's main pork export market, imported 266,225 tonnes of pork from the island in 1996.
In 1982, Japan suspended pork imports from Denmark for 18 months due to foot and mouth disease.

According to a council survey in 1994, the hog industry's net value stood at T$89 billion (US$3.24 billion), comprising 20 percent of Taiwan's farm production value and 60 percent of the livestock value.
Taiwan statistics directorate official Chan Teh-sung said on Saturday the export value of Taiwan's hog industry in 1996 was T$43.6 billion (US$1.55 billion), or 0.5 percent of total GDP.

The island, facing a daunting task in trying to eradicate the disease, was spending US$200 million to import two million doses of vaccine to combat the outbreak, the council said. It had only 50,000 doses on hand when the outbreak was confirmed.

Taiwan's oilseeds importers are considering exporting some of its excessive soymeal production to China to avoid major losses. The crisis could lead to a 10 percent cut of their 2.4 million annual in soybean imports, traders said.
